brief.head: Planner, meet doer
brief.text: Ajay Shah splits himself in two: a planner who sets priorities, and a doer who executes one task fully, missing other deadlines if need be. {091-C01}

brief.head: The fear test
brief.text: Is there anyone in your country you are afraid of? If so, Ajay Shah said, that person has arbitrary power, and something is wrong. {091-C05}

brief.head: Rules beat norms

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on dividing the state
lead.head: No kings, please, we’re a republic
body: Many people behave as if democracy is all about voting, Amit Varma said.
Ajay Shah’s reply set the agenda for the hour. “The essence of democracy is not elections,” he said. “It is in checks and balances. It is in dispersion of power.” {091-C02}

Voting, in his account, only chooses who plays the legislative role. Use it to choose a king and the king could never be unseated, because how could anyone organise an opposition party against a king?

The hosts had covered one way of spreading power, decentralisation, in an earlier episode. This one took up the second: three co-equal branches, a legislature that writes laws, an executive that implements them and a judiciary that settles conflicts.
## Kings and charters
Shah began in the bad old days, when the Emperor Aurangzeb’s power was complete. Rome made the first break: a republic where about fifty families spread power out and set up judges.

The story restarted in England in 1215, when merchants and finance people seized King John. “They put a knife to his throat and they forced him to sign,” Shah said. The document was the Magna Carta. {091-S01}
From there the road ran through Oliver Cromwell to Montesquieu, who proposed cutting the state into three. The clearest expression came, Shah said, in Articles 1, 2 and 3 of the US Constitution.

He made it concrete with a speech offence. Legislators decide whether it is a crime; the police only investigate; only a judge, after hearing both sides, decides on punishment. “To write a law, you gotta win elections,” he said. {091-C03}
As “a stupid economist”, Shah confessed, it took him years to see how powerful this was, because economists tend to picture government as one monolithic thing.
## The Indian detour

India began differently. In the Constituent Assembly, Babasaheb Ambedkar agreed the judiciary must stand apart, but saw no great loss in not separating the executive from the legislature in the American way.

Two later shifts, Varma said, made things worse: Indira Gandhi’s centralisation of power within parties, and the anti-defection law of the late 1980s, which made every MP vote as the whip says. Of the law he said: “Don’t look at intention, look at outcome.”

The result, in Shah’s phrase, is the administrative state, “a world where officials of the executive branch disproportionately exert legislative and judicial powers”. No country, he said, has it worse than India. {091-C06}

Regulators repeat the pattern in miniature. At SEBI, Shah said, one body writes the rules, investigates, prosecutes and judges: “And the judge and the prosecutor and the investigator go have lunch together.” {091-S05}
## Room for hope
Still, Shah was optimistic. Separation of powers was missing from the original text, he said, but it has entered India’s living constitution through the Supreme Court’s basic structure doctrine.
America, meanwhile, is pushing back: in 2024 its Supreme Court largely struck down Chevron deference.
Varma’s worry was atrophy: a party long in power can fill every institution with its own people. The task, he said, is done only when a constitution’s values percolate through society.
Shah agreed that nothing can be taken for granted, and that in India the instinct is still to look for a strongman.
The state, he had said earlier, was never meant to be cosy: “This is not a happy family. This is not a harmonious family. It’s a game of conflict.”

second.label: Party democracy
second.head: Shastri says no to Nehru
second.deck: Amit Varma on the Babri idol and a Congress that once argued
body: When the Ram idol was placed inside the Babri Masjid, Jawaharlal Nehru, in Delhi, ordered it removed within a couple of days, before things got out of hand. {091-S03}

But UP’s chief minister was Govind Ballabh Pant, and his deputy, Lal Bahadur Shastri, who would have had to carry out the order, refused. In that case, Amit Varma said, he wishes they had obeyed Nehru.

His point was about the Congress of the 1950s and 1960s, a grand tent where local politicians could defy the centre and the local party chose its chief minister. That ended in the 1970s, when Indira Gandhi centralised power and the high command began appointing chief ministers. {#indira}

quote.text: Before this you couldn’t freaking appoint a chief minister, the local party would decide it

third.head: Chevron runs out of gas
body: Under Roosevelt, Ajay Shah said, the US federal government built agency upon agency. Nervous Republicans answered with the Administrative Procedure Act of 1946, a single rulebook for every federal agency. {091-C11}

Court orders in a case involving the oil company Chevron later created Chevron deference. If an agency expert had applied her mind and drafted a regulation, judges could review only the process, not the substance. Many saw that as legislative power seeping into the administrative state. {091-S07}
In 2024 the US Supreme Court largely struck it down. “You may be the best expert in the world, you may have 15 PhDs,” Shah said, “but a judge can reopen a matter.”
In a second case, someone argued that the SEC’s in-house judge denied him a jury trial; the Supreme Court struck that arrangement down as unconstitutional.

p2.title: Cutting up the state
p2.deck: Ajay Shah on dispersing power, from the Magna Carta to SEBI, with Amit Varma’s worries about decay

sections.label: The premise
sections.head: Votes don’t make a democracy
sections.caption: democracy as dispersion of power
body: Amit Varma framed the subject with a common belief: that democracy is all about voting. People go to a booth, select a candidate, and the candidate rules over them.
Ajay Shah went further. At heart, he said, democracy is about dispersion of power and checks and balances. Voting is just a way of choosing the people who will play a legislative role. {091-C02}
Used to choose a king, it would produce a ruler impossible to unseat, because nobody could organise an opposition party against a king.
## Two grand ideas

One way to disperse power, Shah said, is decentralisation, covered in an earlier episode: under the subsidiarity principle, each function goes to the lowest level of government that can handle it, with only a few, like foreign policy and military affairs, left to the union.

The second is separation of powers. The state is not a monolithic organisation but three co-equal branches: a legislature that writes laws, an executive that implements them and a judiciary that looks at a conflict and puts out an order. None can override the others.
People who yearn for a strongman, Shah said, find these three branches irritating. But that, he said, is separation of powers.

~ The episode opened with Shah’s personal version of the idea: a planner who plans, then a doer who only does. Varma admired it, while admitting that in his case the planner rocks but the doer is “a frickin’ nikamma”. {#nikamma}

quote.text: It would be a very sad world in which voting was used to choose a king.

sections.label: The history
sections.head: From Aurangzeb to Article 3
sections.caption: how power was prised from kings
body: Ajay Shah started with absolute monarchy: if the Emperor Aurangzeb ordered someone’s head off, there was no choice, and kings allied with religion, as when the Pope crowned Napoleon. {091-J02}

Rome’s republic, the world’s first, spread power out until, in Shah’s words, it “was destroyed by the great man Julius Caesar”. {091-J03} England restarted the story with the Magna Carta in 1215, a road that led to Oliver Cromwell and the beheading of Charles I.
## Three lanes
Then came Montesquieu, whom Shah placed in the 17th century. His proposal was to cut the state vertically into a legislature, an executive and a judiciary, each in its own lane. {#montesquieu}

Shah’s example was a speech offence under the Indian Penal Code. Legislators decide whether it is a crime. {091-C03} Police investigate against the written law. The judge alone decides on punishment, and cannot go after anyone on her own initiative. He called this a mind-blowing achievement in political philosophy.
Amit Varma added that in the US one person investigates and another decides whether to prosecute. That, Shah said, borrowing David Friedman’s phrase, is the machinery of freedom. {091-R01}
~ The ideas found their clearest expression in Articles 1, 2 and 3 of the US Constitution, which set up three co-equal branches with no fear of each other.

quote.text: It was a great day for mankind when these concepts were figured out.

sections.label: The Indian story
sections.head: The executive takes the wheel
sections.caption: India’s executive-heavy state
body: India’s Constituent Assembly debated the question, Ajay Shah said. Professor K.T. Shah moved a resolution, Article 40A, for a clear separation of powers. Babasaheb Ambedkar replied that the executive must be separate from the judiciary, but saw no great loss in not separating it from the legislature. {091-S02}
Amit Varma urged that the choice be judged in context, when the country was falling apart and today’s map did not yet exist.
## The whip hand
Then came the anti-defection law of the late 1980s. Meant to stop horse-trading, it made every MP vote as the whip says. Varma’s verdict: “You could run parliament from an Excel sheet.” {091-J06}
Power within parties, he added, had already been centralised under Indira Gandhi. Together these let a ruling party run both the executive and the legislature from the top. {#combine}

With no MP bothering to read bills, Shah said, the joint secretary writes the law, and district collectors double as district magistrates, a British legacy from when courts were scarce. This is the administrative state. {091-C06}
~ His hope lies in the basic structure doctrine, through which separation of powers has entered India’s living constitution, though a plain reading of the text would not find it. {091-C09}

quote.text: There is no dispute whatsoever that the executive should be separated from the judiciary.
quote.who: Babasaheb Ambedkar, as read by Ajay Shah

sections.label: The regulators
sections.head: A small state inside SEBI
sections.caption: SEBI’s three branches under one roof
body: Before the chapter, Amit Varma reminded Ajay Shah, “explicitly for the camera”, to be kind. {091-J07} Shah, who enormously respects SEBI’s founders, including Surendra Dave and Ravi Narain, still called the original SEBI Act “a really bad piece of work”.
The RBI was created in 1934, mostly as a monetary authority, Shah said; SEBI came in 1992 and copied many of its practices. {#rbi}
## A state in miniature
A regulator’s regulations are laws written by unelected officials, Shah said, and the SEBI Act suffered from what is called excessive delegation. {091-C10}

SEBI also investigates and prosecutes, with the roles mixed up, and then a SEBI employee plays judge. {091-S05} Early orders simply declared someone guilty and imposed a fine of, say, ₹10 crore, with no reasoning. Appeals went to the DEA secretary, who sat on SEBI’s board.

Elsewhere it is cleaner. In Britain and under Australia’s twin-peaks model, the regulator builds a case and takes it to a court or tribunal. At the US SEC, the administrative law judge sits inside the building but belongs to the judiciary.

~ SEBI’s founders put a judge inside in 1992 because they thought the Bombay High Court would never get anything done. XKDR Forum’s recent work, Shah said, shows the Bombay and Delhi High Courts are now reasonably efficient, so the trade-offs may have changed. {091-S06}

quote.text: Regulations are laws. So here you have unelected officials who are drafting law

sections.label: The American turn
sections.head: Even the model needs mending
sections.caption: America’s pushback on its agencies
body: Amit Varma asked whether America, so often the model, had always got separation of powers right. Ajay Shah called the field red hot; the Emerging Markets Conference had held an entire session on it. {091-R07}
Under Roosevelt, the federal government built agencies upon agencies, with Democrats leading the charge. Nervous Republicans pushed for the Administrative Procedure Act of 1946.
## One rulebook

Shah called the APA “a phenomenal piece of work”: a single law setting out checks and balances for every federal agency. The draft Indian Financial Code, on which he worked, did the same, with about 140 sections binding RBI, SEBI and a debt management agency alike. {091-C11}

Varma had earlier predicted that Perplexity could reproduce Shah’s outline. The APA, Shah shot back, is slim but must be read with the thousands of court orders that followed: a law the tool could not parse alone. {091-J08}

Those orders produced Chevron deference, which stopped judges questioning the substance of an expert’s regulation. In 2024 the Supreme Court largely struck it down. {091-S07} Separately, it found the SEC’s in-house trials unconstitutional after someone demanded a jury.
~ Varma took heart from both rulings: they showed, he said, that you can actually move in the right direction.

quote.text: It is one single law that applies to all federal agencies.

sections.label: The afterthoughts
sections.head: Every generation, a new fight
sections.caption: atrophy, vigilance and culture
body: Amit Varma’s worry was atrophy. A well-designed system, he said, decays as politics and incentives take over, and a party long in power can fill every institution with its own people.
Still, separation adds friction. “But when it comes to the state, friction is a good thing,” Varma said: a process guarantees that nothing hasty will be done. {#friction}
It also makes a power grab visible. When Indira Gandhi imposed the Emergency, he said, nobody could pretend democracy was going on. {#emergency}
Hence, in Jefferson’s alleged words, the need for eternal vigilance. {#vigilance}
## Downstream of culture

Varma also warned against treating the Indian Constitution, “well intentioned but deeply flawed”, like a holy book. Politics, he said, quoting Andrew Breitbart, is downstream of culture: liberty lasts when every citizen instinctively objects whenever freedom is infringed. {091-J15}

Ajay Shah agreed that every generation has to fight its own battles. He recalled Angela Merkel saying Germany’s true soul would be known only when the last people who lived through the Second World War had died. In recent elections, he noted, 20 per cent voted for the AfD.
~ For judges, Shah said, the check should be not ministers but peers, lawyers, law bloggers and journals, an argument he credited to the law academic Tarunabh Khaitan. {091-C12}

quote.text: The task of governance and designing a system is not done when you write a constitution.

side.boxText: Montesquieu, Ajay Shah said, drew on earlier thinkers to propose cutting the state vertically into three pieces: legislature, executive and judiciary. Each would keep to its own lane and check the others. Shah placed him in the 17th century. {#montesquieu}

contQuote.text: You and me as the people should never be scared of a person. If you’re scared of somebody, there’s something wrong in your country because that somebody has arbitrary power.

stories.start: So we start in the bad old days, uh, there was monarchy
stories.end: And that's the British journey of reducing the power of the King.
stories.caption: how the king’s power was limited
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how humanity learned to shrink the king
stories.head: A knife at King John’s throat
body: Ajay Shah began in the bad old days of monarchy, when a ruler’s power was complete. If the Emperor Aurangzeb said off with his head, there was no appeal. Kings allied with religion, as when the Pope crowned Napoleon.

The first break came in Rome. There, Shah said, about fifty families took power from concentrated monarchy, spread it out and set up judges. It was the world’s first experiment with a republic, and it “was destroyed by the great man Julius Caesar”. {091-J03}
The story restarted in England in 1215. King John was demanding crazy taxes and loans from a group of merchants and finance people, and they seized him.

“They put a knife to his throat and they forced him to sign a document,” Shah said. The document was the Magna Carta, the Great Charter, the world’s first clear statement of limits on the power of a king. {091-S01}
Read today, he admitted, it seems fossilised. The language is archaic, and it seems to do a few flimsy things. “But you know what? It’s 1215.”

From there the British chipped away at the king’s power through Parliament, until Oliver Cromwell and the beheading of Charles I. People watched, Shah said, and understood that not having an absolute authority is a good thing.
~ That set philosophers debating how to build a state with checks and balances. It led to Montesquieu’s proposal to cut the state in three, and finally to Articles 1, 2 and 3 of the US Constitution.
stories.why: Limits on power were extracted, not gifted, and each step built on people seeing the last one work. Separation of powers, in Shah’s telling, is the mature form of a centuries-old project: nobody should be a king. {091-C05}
stories.postscript: Amit Varma noted that Aristotle also described three branches of government, but as functions of the state, not a separation of powers.

stories.start: SEBI was created in 1992. I enormously respect the individuals who led that work
stories.end: a better separation of powers arrangement as compared to what we have in India
stories.caption: SEBI’s judge, prosecutor and investigator
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a regulator that holds all three powers
stories.head: Three branches, one canteen
body: SEBI was created in 1992 by founders Ajay Shah enormously respects, among them Surendra Dave and Ravi Narain. But it copied practices from the RBI and ended up with all three branches of the state under one roof. {091-S05}

It drafts regulations, which are laws written by unelected officials. It investigates and prosecutes, with the two roles mixed up. Then a SEBI employee plays judge, and his colleague is the prosecutor.
“And the judge and the prosecutor and the investigator go have lunch together,” Shah said, “and they conduct a little trial.”

~ Early orders simply found someone guilty and imposed a fine of, say, ₹10 crore, with no reasoning. Appeals went to the DEA secretary, a SEBI board member. India, Shah reckons, is about 30 per cent of the way to fixing it. {#thirty}
stories.why: Without separation of powers, a regulator quietly becomes a miniature state. The clean design, Shah said, stops the regulator at investigating and deciding whether to prosecute, then hands the case to a real judge. {#clean}

stories.start: Separation of powers was one of the things that was debated.
stories.end: sitting here with the benefit of all that history behind us
stories.caption: Ambedkar’s reply to K.T. Shah
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah reads Ambedkar in the Constituent Assembly
stories.head: No great loss, said Ambedkar
body: The Constituent Assembly debated separation of powers, Ajay Shah said. Professor K.T. Shah moved a resolution, Article 40A, to write a clear separation into the Constitution.

Shah read out the reply of Babasaheb Ambedkar, the assembly’s intellectual luminary. There was no dispute, Ambedkar said, that the executive should be separated from the judiciary. But many Americans were dissatisfied with their own rigid separation of executive and legislature.

The work of Parliament, he argued, was so complicated and vast that its members needed direct guidance from the executive sitting among them. He saw no very great loss, then, in not adopting the American method. {091-S02}

~ So India began with no meaningful separation of powers. Amit Varma asked for context: a country falling apart, its map not yet drawn. The aim, he said, is to learn, not to pass judgment on personalities.
stories.why: India’s executive-heavy state was no accident: its most respected framer chose it deliberately, and gave reasons. The result, Shah said, was that India grew up as a state with extreme executive power. {#executive}

stories.start: many people understood that when a joint secretary writes a law
stories.end: and today there is really no check and balance around these things
stories.caption: Parliament’s standing committees
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a check that lived only in custom
stories.head: A good habit, never written down
body: Many people understood, Ajay Shah said, that a joint secretary writing the laws was a farce. So, starting with Shivraj Patil, a norm grew of sending important bills to parliamentary standing committees. {#patil}
When Shah was in the Ministry of Finance, the Speaker would refer a bill to a committee if it drew significant criticism. No vote was needed.

The committees had ruling and opposition MPs and were always chaired by the opposition. They debated bills, summoned expert witnesses and questioned the civil servants who drafted them. Shah, often an expert witness himself, counts them among the good things behind India’s growth from 1991 to 2011.
~ But the practice was never written into the rules. {091-S04} Today, he said, there is really no check and balance around these things.

quote.text: It was fabulous. It was a great institution. Unfortunately, it was only in norms.

stories.postscript: The lesson, Shah said, is James Buchanan’s public choice reasoning: these things “have to be coded in rules”. {091-C08}

quiz.q: What, according to Ajay Shah, is the essence of democracy, if not elections?
quiz.a: Checks and balances and the dispersion of power; voting only picks legislators.

quiz.q: Who was demanding crazy taxes and loans when merchants put a knife to his throat?
quiz.a: King John of England, who was forced to sign the Magna Carta in 1215.

quiz.q: Which law, by Amit Varma’s account, lets you run Parliament from an Excel sheet?
quiz.a: The anti-defection law of the late 1980s, which makes MPs vote as the whip says.

quiz.q: What American term does Shah use for officials wielding legislative and judicial powers?
quiz.a: The administrative state, and he says no country has it worse than India.

quiz.q: Through which Supreme Court doctrine did separation of powers enter India’s living constitution?
quiz.a: The basic structure doctrine, the amendment-proof core of the Constitution built by judges.

quiz.q: What did the US Supreme Court largely strike down in 2024?
quiz.a: Chevron deference, which stopped judges questioning the substance of an agency’s regulations.
